guides.title: Chemical Water Disinfection & Titration
guides.tags: water, disinfection, chlorine, bleach, iodine, sodis, pathogens, giardia
guides.summary: Neutralize waterborne enteric viruses, bacteria, and amoebic cysts using calculated titrations of sodium hypochlorite (household bleach), tincture of iodine, and solar ultraviolet PET radiation.
guides.content:
## Chemical Disinfection Mechanisms
Pathogens such as *Vibrio cholerae*, *Salmonella typhi*, and hepatitis viruses possess lipid bilayers and enzymes that are destroyed by strong oxidizers. Chlorine (as hypochlorous acid $HOCl$) penetrates bacterial walls and oxidizes sulfhydryl bonds within 30 minutes. **Protozoan cysts (Cryptosporidium and Giardia)** have hard proteinaceous shells that resist low-dose chlorine, requiring extended contact times or mechanical micro-filtration.

```svg
<svg viewBox="0 0 700 380" width="100%" height="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">
  <defs>
    <linearGradient id="waterClr" x1="0%" y1="0%" x2="0%" y2="100%">
      <stop offset="0%" stop-color="#0284c7" stop-opacity="0.3"/>
      <stop offset="100%" stop-color="#0369a1" stop-opacity="0.6"/>
    </linearGradient>
  </defs>

  <rect x="0" y="0" width="700" height="380" fill="#090d16" rx="8"/>

  <!-- Method 1: Household Bleach (NaOCl 5-8%) -->
  <g transform="translate(30, 25)">

    <text x="100" y="26" fill="#38bdf8" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" font-family="monospace" text-anchor="middle">BLEACH (5-8.25%)</text>

    <text x="25" y="160" fill="#64748b" font-size="9.5" font-family="monospace">• Direct sunlight only</text>

    <!-- Overcast Spec -->
    <rect x="15" y="176" width="170" height="60" rx="5" fill="#1e293b"/>
    <text x="25" y="193" fill="#94a3b8" font-size="10" font-family="monospace">OVERCAST / CLOUDY:</text>
    <text x="25" y="213" fill="#f59e0b" font-size="14" font-weight="bold" font-family="monospace">48 Hours (2 Days)</text>
    <text x="25" y="228" fill="#64748b" font-size="9.5" font-family="monospace">• Extended UV contact</text>

    <text x="100" y="258" fill="#a7f3d0" font-size="10" font-family="monospace" text-anchor="middle">PET Bottle (< 2L) Only</text>
  </g>

  <!-- Bottom Verification Rule (Clean 2-Line Box) -->
  <rect x="25" y="318" width="650" height="46" rx="6" fill="#1e293b" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="1"/>
  <text x="350" y="336" fill="#f8fafc" font-size="11" font-weight="bold" font-family="monospace" text-anchor="middle">THE SNIFF TEST: Treated water MUST smell faintly of chlorine after 30 mins.</text>
  <text x="350" y="352" fill="#fca5a5" font-size="10" font-family="monospace" text-anchor="middle">If no faint chlorine odor is detected, repeat dose & wait an additional 15 mins.</text>
</svg>
```

## Protocol Dosing & Titration Tables
1. **Sodium Hypochlorite (Household Bleach):**
   - Check label: Ensure it is **unscented regular bleach with NO detergents or corrosion inhibitors** ($5.25\%\text{ to }8.25\%\text{ NaOCl}$).
   - *Clear Water:* Add **2 drops per liter** (or 8 drops per gallon).
   - *Turbid / Floodwater:* Pre-filter through cloth, then add **4 drops per liter** (16 drops per gallon).
   - *Reaction Wait:* Agitate vigorously. Let stand for **30 minutes**. Water must have a slight residual chlorine odor. If no odor is present, repeat the dose and wait an additional 15 minutes.
2. **Tincture of Iodine (2% USP):**
   - Add **5 drops per liter** for clear water ($20\text{ drops per gallon}$).
   - For icy cold river water ($<10^\circ\text{C}$), double dose to **10 drops per liter** and wait **60 minutes**.
   - *Contraindication:* Do not use continuously for more than 3 weeks; avoid in pregnant individuals and those with thyroid disorders.
3. **SODIS (Solar Disinfection):**
   - Fill clear PET plastic beverage bottles ($<2\text{ liters}$; bottle must be clear and scratch-free).
   - Shake vigorously for 20 seconds to oxygenate water (oxygen radicals enhance UV cell lysis).
   - Lay flat on a corrugated galvanized iron roof. UV-A rays ($320–400\text{ nm}$) plus solar heating ($>50^\circ\text{C}$) sanitize bacteria within **6 hours of direct sunlight**.

guides.title: Dakota Fire Hole & Friction Fire
guides.tags: fire, combustion, stealth, convection, windproof, thermal efficiency
guides.summary: Excavate a two-chamber subterranean convective hearth that burns hot, produces virtually zero visible smoke, shields against high winds, and supports cooking pots directly over ground level.
guides.content:
## Aerodynamic Principle
The Dakota Fire Hole utilizes **thermal draft convection**. Burning wood in the primary chamber heats air, creating an aggressive low-pressure updraft. As rising hot air exhausts through the vertical combustion chimney, it forces fresh cold oxygen-rich air to rush down the angled feeder tunnel, creating an automated bellows effect that sustains temperatures exceeding **700°C** with minimal fuel.

```svg
</svg>
```

## Excavation & Operational Procedure
1. **Locate Wind Direction:** Determine the prevailing surface wind. The air intake tunnel MUST be dug upwind of the fire chamber.
2. **Excavate Primary Chamber:** Dig a circular hole 30 cm (12 in) wide and 30–40 cm deep with vertical walls.
3. **Excavate Air Shaft:** Step 30 cm upwind and dig a second hole 20 cm wide, angled diagonally at 45 degrees downward until it punctures into the bottom base of the combustion chamber.
4. **Draft Test:** Drop a piece of smoldering dry tinder into the air shaft; smoke should instantly suck down through the tunnel and eject straight out the fire pit.
5. **Lighting & Fueling:** Build a small tinder nest at the base of the fire chamber. Ignite and feed with pencil-lead sized dry twigs, gradually increasing to thumb-thickness hardwood sticks.
6. **Zero-Trace Extinguishment:** When finished, rake coals flat, fill both holes with the excavated dirt, and replace the top sod plug. No surface scorch mark or coal remains visible.

guides.title: Debris Hut Insulative Shelter
guides.tags: shelter, debris hut, insulation, hypothermia, thermal envelope
guides.summary: Construct an individual thermal cocoon utilizing a ridgepole, rib struts, and a 1-meter thick compressed leaf/moss insulation layer capable of preventing fatal hypothermia down to sub-zero temperatures.
guides.content:
## Physical Thermal Principle
Human body heat is lost predominantly through **conduction to the frozen earth** and **convection via ambient wind**. A debris hut traps body heat within a minimal micro-volume by creating an envelope of thousands of dead-air pockets. The interior space must be just large enough to fit your body tightly; extra space demands extra caloric energy to heat.

## Construction Rules
1. **Ridgepole Selection:** Secure a sturdy deadfall timber roughly 1.5x your body length (3 meters) and 10–12 cm thick. Test under full body weight.
2. **Support Apex:** Wedge the front end into the fork of a tree or onto an interlocking two-branch bipod at roughly waist height (0.8 to 1 meter). The tail rests directly on the earth facing into prevailing winds.
3. **Rib Skeleton:** Lean hundreds of sturdy branches along both sides of the ridgepole at a 45-degree angle, spaced no more than hand-width apart.
4. **Lattice Webbing:** Weave flexible twigs, dry ferns, and vines horizontally over the ribs to create a net so small debris does not fall into the sleeping cavity.
5. **Bedding Layer:** Pack the interior floor with **at least 30 cm (1 foot)** of dry leaves, dry grass, or moss. An uninsulated floor will leech all body heat via ground conduction.
6. **Thick Outer Insulation:** Pile dry forest debris (leaves, needles, dry moss, duff) over the exterior to a depth of **at least 1 meter (arm's length)**.
7. **Door Plug:** Gather an armful of leaves or a backpack to seal the entrance after sliding in feet first.

guides.title: Mastery of Fire: 5 Alternative Fire-Starting Methods for Any Situation
guides.tags: fire, friction, bow drill, flint and steel, lens, chemical, survival, thermal
guides.summary: Complete practical manual covering 5 distinct methods of generating fire without matches or lighters: friction bow drill, percussion flint & steel, optical lens concentration, electrical short-circuit, and chemical ignition.
guides.content:
Fire is the primary catalyst of human civilization. It provides thermoregulation against hypothermia, sanitizes drinking water through boiling, renders calories digestible, deters predatory wildlife, hardens wooden tools, and serves as the thermal foundation for metallurgy and ceramics.

In survival and rebuild scenarios, relying on a single ignition tool (such as matches or butane lighters) guarantees eventual failure. You must master fire generation across five distinct physical and chemical mechanisms depending on weather, salvaged materials, and environmental moisture.

```
       5 PRIMARY FIRE GENERATION MECHANISMS
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ 1. MECHANICAL FRICTION  → Wood cellular abrasion      │
│ 2. PERCUSSION SPARK     → Pyrophoric metal oxidation   │
│ 3. OPTICAL CONCENTRATION→ Solar radiant focus          │
│ 4. ELECTRICAL SHORT     → Resistive Joule heating      │
│ 5. CHEMICAL REACTION    → Exothermic redox reaction    │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

---

### Method 1: The Bow Drill (Mechanical Wood Friction)

The bow drill is the most reliable primitive method worldwide. It converts mechanical reciprocal arm motion into continuous rotational friction, heating powdered wood dust above its auto-ignition temperature (approx. $400^\circ\text{C}$ / $750^\circ\text{F}$) to form a smoldering ember.

#### 1. Material Selection (The Anatomy of the Set)
* **Hearth Board (Base):** Non-resinous, medium-soft, dry dead wood. Test with thumbnail: if it leaves a distinct depression without crumbling, it is ideal. *Optimal species:* Cedar, Basswood, Willow, Aspen, Cottonwood, Yucca. *Strictly avoid:* Pine, Fir, Spruce (resins melt and glaze into a frictionless lubricant).
* **Spindle (Drill):** Straight, finger-thick (2 cm diameter) round branch of the same wood species, 20 cm long. Carve top into a steep, low-friction point; carve bottom into a blunt, high-friction 45° taper.
* **Bow:** Curved, stiff green branch or strong hardwood stick, 60–75 cm long, finger-thick. String with 550 paracord, rawhide, braided inner tree bark (cedar/willow), or bootlaces.
* **Bearing Block (Handhold):** Hard dense hardwood, smooth stone with a natural depression, or lubricated bone/seashell. Lubricate socket with pine needle oil, facial grease, or green leaves to eliminate friction at the top handhold.
* **Tinder Bundle (Bird's Nest):** Fine, desiccated fiber: dry cedar bark buffed between hands, dried grass, cattail down, crushed thistle pith.

#### 2. Mechanical Blueprint & Setup

<svg viewBox="0 0 700 360" width="100%" height="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">
  <rect width="700" height="360" fill="#0d1117" rx="12"/>
  <rect x="20" y="20" width="660" height="320" fill="#161b22" rx="8" stroke="#30363d" stroke-width="1"/>
  
  <text x="350" y="45" font-family="monospace" font-size="14" font-weight="bold" fill="#f59e0b" text-anchor="middle">BOW DRILL FRICTION ARCHITECTURE</text>
  
  <!-- Bearing Block -->
  <path d="M 310 70 L 390 70 L 375 105 L 325 105 Z" fill="#78350f" stroke="#d97706" stroke-width="1.5"/>
  <text x="405" y="90" font-family="monospace" font-size="11" fill="#cbd5e1">Bearing Block (Greased)</text>

  <rect x="340" y="105" width="20" height="150" fill="#b45309" stroke="#f59e0b" stroke-width="1.5" rx="3"/>

  <!-- Bow & Cord -->
  <path d="M 120 220 Q 300 80 500 200" fill="none" stroke="#92400e" stroke-width="6"/>
  <path d="M 130 215 L 340 185 L 360 185 L 490 195" fill="none" stroke="#ef4444" stroke-width="2.5" stroke-dasharray="3,3"/>

  <rect x="240" y="255" width="220" height="30" fill="#78350f" stroke="#d97706" stroke-width="1.5" rx="2"/>
  <text x="480" y="275" font-family="monospace" font-size="11" fill="#cbd5e1">Hearth Board (Softwood)</text>
  
  <!-- Notch & Dust Collector -->
  <polygon points="340,255 360,255 350,285" fill="#0d1117"/>

  <text x="350" y="330" font-family="monospace" font-size="9" fill="#94a3b8" text-anchor="middle">V-Notch cut 1/8th pie slice into burn circle</text>
</svg>

#### 3. Execution Protocol
1. **Burn-in:** Carve a small dimple 1 cm from the edge of the hearth board. Loop spindle into bow cord (single twist). Place left foot firmly on the hearth board. Lock left wrist against left shin to hold bearing block vertical. Drill with slow, steady strokes until spindle tip burns a black depression.
2. **Carve the Notch:** Stop drilling. Cut a clean V-shaped notch (approx. 45° to 60° angle) from the outer edge of the board into the exact center of the burn circle. Place a thin dry leaf or bark slice under the notch to collect dust.
3. **The Coal Run:** Resume drilling. Begin with long, smooth, rhythmic strokes using the full length of the bow. Once dense, thick white smoke pours from the notch, increase downward pressure slightly and accelerate stroke rate for 15–20 seconds until pungent dark-brown/black dust fills the notch.
4. **Coal Separation:** Stop drilling. Gently tap the board. A steady stream of self-sustaining smoke must rise from the accumulated dust pile. Fan gently with hand until an orange glowing coal appears.
5. **Transfer to Tinder:** Tip the coal into the prepared bird's nest. Fold tinder gently around the ember without suffocating it. Hold at eye level facing into the breeze and blow with long, steady, expanding breaths until the bundle ignites in flame.

---

### Method 2: Percussion (Flint & High-Carbon Steel)

Flint and steel does not generate sparks from the stone; rather, the sharp, hard flint (hardness 7 on Mohs scale) shears microscopic particles of iron from the high-carbon steel striker (carbon content $>0.7\%$). The intense friction and mechanical shear energy tear off pyrophoric iron shavings that instantaneously combust in atmospheric oxygen at $1,100^\circ\text{C}$ ($2,000^\circ\text{F}$).

#### 1. Required Components
* **High-Carbon Steel:** Old metal files, carbon steel knife spines, or forged C-strikers. *Stainless steel will NOT work* (chromium inhibits pyrophoric ignition).
* **Hard Sharp Rock:** Chert, flint, jasper, chalcedony, quartz, or fractured obsidian.
* **Char Cloth (Low-Temperature Pyrolysis Tinder):** 100% plant fiber (cotton canvas, denim, linen) heated inside an airtight metal tin with a single pinhole until volatile gases vent and burn off, leaving pure fragile carbonized cloth that catches the faintest micro-spark.

#### 2. Striking Protocol
1. Place a 3x3 cm square of char cloth flat on top of the flint flake, flush with the razor-sharp edge (leaving 1 mm exposed).
2. Hold flint and cloth firmly between thumb and forefinger.
3. Strike the high-carbon steel downward across the sharp rock edge at a steep 30° glancing angle. The steel must glance off the rock edge, not hit it dead-on.
4. Tiny orange sparks will curl backward and land onto the char cloth. An ember will immediately begin to glow and propagate outward across the woven carbon grid.
5. Transfer the glowing char cloth into the center of a dry tinder bundle and blow into flame.

---

### Method 3: Optical Refraction & Solar Concentration

When high-intensity direct sunlight is available, optical lenses concentrate parallel solar radiation to a pin-point focal point, creating temperatures exceeding $500^\circ\text{C}$ in seconds.

#### 1. Usable Optical Mediums
* **Convex Glass Magnifying Lens:** 50mm+ diameter double-convex lens.
* **Salvaged Optics:** Camera lenses, binocular eyepieces, telescope lenses, or eyeglasses designed for *farsightedness* (presbyopia/hyperopia). *Nearsighted glasses are concave and disperse light.*
* **Improvised Clear Water Bulb:** A spherical clear incandescent lightbulb or clear transparent plastic wrap filled with water and twisted into an air-free sphere acts as a short-focal-length water lens.
* **Shaped Ice Lens:** In freezing climates, cut a thick chunk of pure, air-bubble-free ice from a pond or lake. Use the warmth of cupped hands to shape and polish the ice into a smooth, double-convex lens (thicker in center, thin at rims). The ice concentrates light without melting prematurely.

#### 2. Focusing Procedure
1. Prepare a dark, powdery target tinder: dry char cloth, shredded punk wood (decayed dry heartwood), dried crushed herbivore dung, or charred cotton. Dark pigments absorb maximum radiant photon energy.
2. Direct the lens perpendicular to the sun's rays.
3. Adjust distance between lens and tinder until the circle of light shrinks to the absolute smallest, blindingly bright pinhead point.
4. Hold completely motionless for 30–60 seconds. A thin column of white smoke will appear, followed by a glowing red coal inside the tinder dust.

---

### Method 4: Electrical Short-Circuit & Joule Heating

Electrical energy stored in chemical cells (batteries) can be converted to instantaneous thermal energy via high-current short-circuit across high-resistance conductive elements ($P = I^2 R$).

#### 1. Techniques & Setups
* **Method A: Steel Wool & 9V / 12V Battery**
  - Fine grade steel wool (0000 or 000 grade) consists of microscopic carbon-steel fibers.
  - Touching both terminals of a standard 9V battery (or wires from a 12V car battery) directly to the steel wool causes current to surge through the thin strands. The resistance causes the steel filaments to ignite and burn across the pad at over $700^\circ\text{C}$.
  - Immediately feed dry shredded cedar bark or fine grass into the burning wool.
* **Method B: Pencil Lead (Graphite) & Vehicle Battery**
  - Remove wood from a common #2 pencil to extract the continuous graphite rod (graphite is an electrical conductor with high resistance).
  - Connect two insulated copper wires to vehicle battery terminals ($+$ and $-$).
  - Touch both bare wire ends to the graphite rod 2 cm apart. Within 3 seconds, the graphite will glow white-hot, instantly igniting tinder pressed against it.
* **Method C: Chewing Gum Foil Wrapper & 1.5V AA Battery**
  - Cut a foil-backed paper gum wrapper into an hourglass shape (wide at ends, narrowed to a 1.5–2 mm bridge at center).
  - Press the metallic foil side against the positive and negative ends of an AA or AAA cell.
  - Current density concentrates at the narrow bridge; within 1 second, the paper bridge combusts into an open flame.

---

### Method 5: Chemical Hypergolic Oxidation

Chemical ignition requires zero arm exertion and operates in damp or freezing conditions. It relies on combining an aggressive oxidizing agent with a volatile organic fuel.

#### 1. Potassium Permanganate ($KMnO_4$) + Glycerin
* **Chemical Principle:** Potassium permanganate is a powerful oxidizer. Glycerol (glycerin, found in medical lotions and automotive antifreeze) is a readily oxidizable polyol. Their mixture undergoes an escalating exothermic redox reaction:
  $$14KMnO_4 + 4C_3H_5(OH)_3 \to 7K_2CO_3 + 7Mn_2O_3 + 5CO_2 \uparrow + 16H_2O + \text{Intense Heat}$$
* **Field Procedure:**
  1. Place 1 teaspoon of finely ground purple $KMnO_4$ crystals into a small pile on a dry stone or wood scrap.
  2. Depress the center of the pile to create a small crater.
  3. Add 4–5 drops of pure liquid glycerin into the crater.
  4. Step back 1 meter. A slow reaction will begin: white fumes will emit for 20–40 seconds as temperature climbs exponentially, followed by a spontaneous, violent purple flame reaching $1,000^\circ\text{C}$.
  5. Place dry twig kindling directly over the flame.

---

### Situational Selection Matrix

| Survival Situation | Best Method | Secondary Backup | Strict Avoidance |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Soaking Wet Rain / Humid Jungle** | Chemical ($KMnO_4$ + Glycerin) or Steel Wool + Battery | Bow Drill (using dry dead standing cedar heartwood) | Flint & Steel without waterproofed char cloth |
| **Arid / Sunny Desert** | Optical Lens Concentration | Bow Drill (Yucca on Yucca) | Battery short (waste of stored electrical reserves) |
| **Sub-Zero Arctic / Snowfield** | Shaped Ice Lens or Percussion | Bow drill with fat-greased bearing block | Cold gum-wrapper battery (frozen electrolytes drop output) |
| **Long-Term Off-Grid Settlement** | Flint & High-Carbon Steel + Char Cloth | Fire Piston / Bow Drill | Chemical kits (non-renewable reagents) |

guides.title: Field Trauma Stabilization: Hemorrhage, Splinting, Airway & Chest Wounds
guides.tags: trauma, first aid, tourniquet, chest seal, splint, shock, medical, emergency
guides.summary: Field protocol for managing immediate life-threatening injuries when emergency medical services are nonexistent: wound packing, three-sided chest seal for sucking chest wounds, improvised traction splints, and hypovolemic shock resuscitation.
guides.content:
In a collapsed infrastructure environment, traumatic injury (from debris, falling timber, physical violence, or mechanical failure) is the leading cause of preventable mortality within the first 60 minutes. Without paramedics or surgical units, emergency first responders must execute the military **M.A.R.C.H.** protocol in strict sequence:

```
  THE M.A.R.C.H. TRIAGE SEQUENCE
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ M - Massive Bleeding   → Occlude arterial hemorrhage   │
│ A - Airway             → Clear obstructions & position │
│ R - Respiration        → Seal open pneumothorax wounds │
│ C - Circulation        → Stabilize shock & splint breaks│
│ H - Hypothermia / Head → Insulate and preserve heat    │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

---

### Step 1: Massive Hemorrhage Control

Blood loss from a lacerated femoral, brachial, or carotid artery can cause fatal hypovolemic shock within 90 to 180 seconds.

#### 1. Extremity Bleeding (Arms and Legs)
* **Primary Intervention:** Windlass Tourniquet applied 5–7 cm proximal to the wound (never over a joint). If the bleeding location is obscured by clothing or darkness, place the tourniquet "high and tight" at the root of the limb.
* **Tightening Metric:** Twist windlass until bright-red pulsatile bleeding ceases completely and the distal peripheral pulse (wrist radial or ankle tibial) is absent. Lock the windlass rod securely.

#### 2. Junctional Bleeding (Groin, Axilla/Armpit, Neck)
Tourniquets cannot compress junctional wounds.
* **Technique (Wound Packing):**
  1. Clear clotted blood from the wound cavity using fingers.
  2. Take clean sterile gauze (or strips of boiled cotton fabric).
  3. Form a small "ball" of gauze at the end of the roll and press it with a finger directly against the bleeding vessel bone interface at the base of the wound cavity.
  4. Continue feeding gauze tightly into the cavity under continuous finger pressure until the entire cavity is tightly packed like concrete.
  5. Apply full body-weight manual pressure directly over the packed cavity for a minimum of **3 continuous minutes** (for hemostatic gauze) or **10 continuous minutes** (for plain gauze).
  6. Secure with a compressive pressure wrap anchored with a tight knot.

---

### Step 2: Open Sucking Chest Wound & Tension Pneumothorax

Penetrating trauma to the thoracic cage (stab, shrapnel, puncture) disrupts negative intrapleural pressure. With every inhalation, atmospheric air is drawn through the chest wall into the pleural cavity rather than into the lung, collapsing the lung and creating pressure that eventually kinks the vena cava, causing cardiac arrest.

#### 1. The Vented Flutter Seal Blueprint

<svg viewBox="0 0 700 360" width="100%" height="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">
  <rect width="700" height="360" fill="#0d1117" rx="12"/>
  <rect x="20" y="20" width="660" height="320" fill="#161b22" rx="8" stroke="#30363d" stroke-width="1"/>
  
  <text x="350" y="45" font-family="monospace" font-size="14" font-weight="bold" fill="#ef4444" text-anchor="middle">IMPROVISED THREE-SIDED FLUTTER CHEST SEAL</text>
  
  <!-- Chest Wall Skin -->
  <rect x="180" y="80" width="340" height="220" fill="#292524" stroke="#57534e" stroke-width="2" rx="8"/>
  <text x="350" y="105" font-family="monospace" font-size="12" fill="#a8a29e" text-anchor="middle">Thoracic Chest Wall</text>
  
  <!-- Penetrating Wound -->
  <ellipse cx="350" cy="190" rx="15" ry="25" fill="#7f1d1d" stroke="#ef4444" stroke-width="2"/>
  <text x="350" y="195" font-family="monospace" font-size="9" fill="#fca5a5" text-anchor="middle">Puncture</text>
  
  <!-- Plastic Sheet (Occlusive Barrier) -->
  <rect x="270" y="130" width="160" height="130" fill="#38bdf8" opacity="0.3" stroke="#38bdf8" stroke-width="1.5" stroke-dasharray="4,2"/>
  <text x="350" y="150" font-family="monospace" font-size="11" fill="#7dd3fc" text-anchor="middle">Airtight Plastic Foil</text>
  
  <!-- Tape On 3 Sides -->
  <rect x="260" y="125" width="180" height="12" fill="#eab308" stroke="#ca8a04" stroke-width="1"/>
  <rect x="260" y="125" width="12" height="140" fill="#eab308" stroke="#ca8a04" stroke-width="1"/>
  <rect x="428" y="125" width="12" height="140" fill="#eab308" stroke="#ca8a04" stroke-width="1"/>
  
  <text x="350" y="120" font-family="monospace" font-size="9" fill="#fde047" text-anchor="middle">Top Tape Strip (Sealed)</text>
  <text x="210" y="195" font-family="monospace" font-size="9" fill="#fde047" text-anchor="middle">Left Tape</text>
  <text x="490" y="195" font-family="monospace" font-size="9" fill="#fde047" text-anchor="middle">Right Tape</text>
  
  <!-- Bottom Flutter Valve (Open) -->
  <line x1="260" y1="265" x2="440" y2="265" stroke="#ef4444" stroke-width="2" stroke-dasharray="6,4"/>
  <text x="350" y="285" font-family="monospace" font-size="11" fill="#4ade80" font-weight="bold" text-anchor="middle">BOTTOM UNTAPED (ONE-WAY FLUTTER VALVE)</text>
  <text x="350" y="300" font-family="monospace" font-size="9" fill="#cbd5e1" text-anchor="middle">Inhalation: Plastic sucks flat, sealing air out</text>
  <text x="350" y="315" font-family="monospace" font-size="9" fill="#cbd5e1" text-anchor="middle">Exhalation: Trapped pleural air vents out bottom</text>
</svg>

#### 2. Improvised Dressing Procedure
1. Find any clean, airtight plastic sheet: heavy-duty plastic packaging, resealable freezer bag, or clean laminated foil.
2. Cut into a square (approx. 15x15 cm) that extends at least 5 cm beyond the wound perimeter in all directions.
3. Clean gross blood and sweat from skin around the wound.
4. Place plastic square over the wound.
5. Apply heavy adhesive tape (duct tape, surgical tape) along **three sides only**. Leave the bottom edge completely open.
6. **Operating Dynamics:**
   - On **Inhalation**, negative pressure draws the plastic flat against the chest wall, hermetically sealing the wound and preventing air entry into the pleural space.
   - On **Exhalation**, escaping pleural air and blood force the unsealed bottom flap outward, allowing pressurized air to vent freely.
7. **Needle Decompression Fallback:** If the patient develops severe cyanosis, tracheal deviation away from the affected side, and absent breath sounds (tension pneumothorax), vent the flap immediately. If still unrelieved, insert a sterile, large-bore needle (14-gauge) into the 2nd intercostal space along the mid-clavicular line directly above the 3rd rib to vent trapped high-pressure gas.

---

### Step 3: Musculoskeletal Fracture Immobilization & Splinting

Unstable bone fractures lacerate neighboring arteries and sever nerve trunks during movement. Rigid splinting eliminates micro-movement, alleviates agony, and prevents closed fractures from piercing the skin into compound injuries.

#### 1. Splinting Rules of Order
* **Check Distal Circulation, Sensation, and Motor (CSM) function** at fingers or toes before and after applying any splint. If pulse disappears after splinting, loosen the lashing immediately.
* **Immobilize the joint above AND the joint below** the fracture site (e.g., for a mid-shaft tibia fracture, immobilize both the knee and the ankle).
* **Pad All Voids:** Wrap dense padding (clothing, dry moss, foam) between the splint and bony prominences (ankles, knees, elbows) to prevent pressure necrosis.

#### 2. Fracture Variants & Improvised Splints
* **Rigid Branch/Board Splint:** Place two straight, sturdy wooden slats on the lateral and medial sides of the limb. Anchor with at least four circumferential cloth ties (two above the break, two below the break).
* **Anatomic (Buddy) Splinting:** When no materials exist, bind the fractured limb to the patient's healthy anatomy:
  - Fractured finger taped to adjacent healthy finger.
  - Fractured leg bound firmly to the uninjured leg using four wide cloth wraps.
  - Fractured arm bound against the torso using a sling and swathe wrap.
* **Improvised Hare Traction Splint (for Femur Fractures):**
  - A fractured femur causes violent spasms of the large quadriceps muscle, driving broken bone ends past each other with massive internal hemorrhage (1–2 liters).
  - Notch a long branch (extending from hip to 20 cm past the foot). Anchor top to pelvis with a groin strap. Anchor bottom to ankle hitch. Use a Spanish windlass stick at the foot to exert continuous longitudinal axial traction until limb lengths are symmetrical.

---

### Step 4: Hypovolemic Shock Management & Oral Hydration

Shock is acute systemic hypoperfusion where cellular metabolic demands exceed tissue oxygen delivery.

#### 1. Early Warning Diagnostics
* Heart rate $>100\,\text{bpm}$ with weak, thready pulse.
* Capillary refill time $>2$ seconds (press fingernail bed until white; time to pink return).
* Cold, pale, clammy skin; rapid shallow respiration; confusion or restlessness.

#### 2. Resuscitation Protocol
1. **Arrest All Bleeding:** Re-check tourniquets and pressure dressings.
2. **Thermal Conservation:** Strip wet clothing. Wrap patient in dry blankets, wool, or space blankets. Insulate underneath the patient from the cold ground using pine boughs or sleeping pads. *Hypothermic blood cannot form stable fibrin clots.*
3. **Trendelenburg / Recovery Positioning:** Elevate legs 20–30 cm above heart level (autotransfusion of 300–500 mL venous reserve) unless chest trauma or head injury is present.
4. **WHO Oral Rehydration Salt (ORS) Formulation:** If patient is conscious and can swallow, avoid pure water (which causes hyponatremia and cellular swelling). Administer isotonic ORS:
   $$\text{Water: } 1.0\,\text{Liter} \quad|\quad \text{Table Salt } (NaCl)\text{: } 2.5\,\text{g (0.5 tsp)} \quad|\quad \text{Sugar/Honey: } 30.0\,\text{g (6 tsp)}$$
   The sodium-glucose co-transport mechanism in the intestinal mucosa rapidly absorbs water and sodium directly into the bloodstream without osmotic diarrhea.

guides.title: Critical Survival Knots & Lashings
guides.tags: knots, rigging, cordage, shelter, lashing, rescue, bowline
guides.summary: Master the four non-negotiable mechanical friction knots and timber lashings required for structural shelters, litter evacuations, tarp tensioning, and ascending ropes.
guides.content:
## Mechanical Friction & Jam-Proofing Principles
In high-stress rescue and construction scenarios, poor knots either slip under dynamic shock loads or weld permanently tight under tension. A true survival knot retains **60% to 80% of native rope strength**, resists unintentional release, yet can be untied effortlessly after bearing human body weight.

## Step-by-Step Tying Procedures
1. **The Bowline ("The King of Knots"):**
   - Form a small eyelet loop in the standing part (the "rabbit hole").
   - Pass the working end up through the hole (the "rabbit comes out of the hole").
   - Pass around behind the main standing line (the "rabbit runs around the tree").
   - Pass back down into the initial loop (the "rabbit goes back down the hole").
   - Pull working end and standing line firmly. The loop will never slip or tighten down around a victim.
2. **Taut-Line Hitch (Adjustable Tensioner):**
   - Wrap working end around anchor post and bring back parallel to the standing line.
   - Make two consecutive wraps inside the loop progressing toward the anchor.
   - Cross over and make one final half-hitch outside the loop away from the anchor.
   - Slide the friction barrel along the rope to tighten tent guylines against high storm winds.
3. **The Prusik Hitch (Friction Ascender):**
   - Tie a closed loop of thinner cord (5–6 mm) using a double fisherman's knot.
   - Wrap the loop three times around a thicker host rope (9–12 mm), passing through its own center each pass.
   - Dress wraps so they lie neat and flat. When weighted downwards, the cord bites into the main rope; unweighted, it slides freely up or down for self-rescue climbing.
4. **Square Lashing (Structural Timber):**
   - Start with a clove hitch on the vertical spar below the crossbar.
   - Wrap three times around both timbers alternately (over horizontal, under vertical).
   - Apply two tight "frapping turns" *between* the timbers to cinch cordage to maximum tension. Finish with a clove hitch.

guides.content:
When modern ammunition is exhausted, firearms become nothing more than heavy iron clubs. The bow is the premier silent hunting weapon and perimeter defense tool of human history. A well-tillered **50-pound (23 kg) longbow** propels a 500-grain broadhead arrow at **160 feet per second (50 m/s)**, delivering over 40 foot-pounds of kinetic energy—sufficient to achieve complete pass-through penetration on large cervids (deer, elk, wild boar) and deter predatory wildlife silently at ranges out to 40 meters.

---

## 1. Wood Selection & The Anatomy of a Longbow

A bow is a mechanical leaf spring. When you pull the bowstring:
- The **Back** (the side facing the target) is stretched under intense **tensile stress**.
- The **Belly** (the side facing the archer) is crushed under intense **compressive stress**.

| Timber Species | Density ($g/cm^3$) | Tensile Strength | Compressive Strength | Bowyer Characteristics |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :--- |
| **Osage Orange (*Maclura pomifera*)** | $0.85$ | Extreme | Indestructible | The gold standard; dense yellow heartwood, virtually unbreakable |
| **Shagbark Hickory (*Carya ovata*)** | $0.78$ | Immense | Good | Best tension back; resists splintering even when green |
| **White Ash (*Fraxinus americana*)** | $0.67$ | Excellent | Moderate | Straight-grained, lightweight, easy to tiller, fast arrow cast |
| **Pacific Yew (*Taxus brevifolia*)** | $0.64$ | High | Supreme | Traditional English longbow wood: white sapwood back + red heartwood belly |

### Sourcing & Splitting:
1. Harvest a straight, knot-free sapling or log, **1.8 meters (6 feet) long and 10 to 15 cm in diameter**.
2. Split lengthwise with wooden wedges and a mallet into four triangular quarters (staves).
3. **The Single Growth Ring Rule:** Debark the stave carefully with a wooden scraper. Choose a single continuous growth ring on the exterior wood surface to serve as the **Back of the bow**. Never cut, nick, or gouge this ring; if an edge grain is violated, the tension forces at full draw will peel the wood fiber, causing the bow to snap in half violently.

---

## 2. Tillering: The Art of Balanced Limb Flexure

Tillering is the methodical removal of wood from the **belly** so that both limbs bend in an identical, harmonious parabolic curve.

1. **Rough Dimensions:**
   - Total Length: **175 cm (68 inches)**.
   - Handle Grip: 10 cm in the center, 28 mm wide and 32 mm thick.
   - Limbs: Taper from 40 mm wide near the handle down to 15 mm at the tips.
2. **Floor Tillering:** Rest the bottom tip on the ground. Hold the handle with one hand and push down on the upper tip. Observe where the limb bends. If it feels stiff, scrape thin shavings off the belly with a cabinet scraper, glass shard, or draw-knife.
3. **The Tillering Stick:**
   - Construct a vertical wooden board notched with notches every 25 mm from 15 cm down to 70 cm (28 inches, full draw length).
   - Place the bow handle in the top saddle. Hook a long tillering string to the nocks.
   - Pull the string down notch by notch. Step back 4 paces and inspect the curvature:
     - *Hinges (Weak spots bending too sharply):* **Do not touch them!** Mark them with charcoal.
     - *Stiff spots (Straight segments):* Scrape wood off the belly only along these stiff segments.
4. **Target Draw Weight:** When both limbs bend in a mirror-image elliptical arc to a full **28-inch draw** while requiring **50 pounds (23 kg)** of scale force, tillering is complete.
5. **Heat Treating the Belly (Tempering):** Clamp the bow backwards into a slight reflex curve. Sweep a hot charcoal bed or blowtorch flame along the belly until the wood turns light golden-brown. This hardens the wood cellular structure, increasing compressive stiffness and preventing the bow from "taking set" (permanently losing springiness).

---

## 3. Fabricating Flemish Twist Bowstrings

A bowstring must withstand 200+ pounds of shock load without stretching. Modern Dacron or FastFlight is ideal, but in the wilderness, you must harvest high-tensile bast fibers:

1. **Fiber Harvesting:** Extract long bast fibers from the inner bark of **Stinging Nettle, Dogbane (Indian Hemp), Flax, or Wild Hemp**. Alternatively, shred dried back sinew from deer or cattle into silken threads.
2. **Waxing:** Rub the fiber bundles vigorously with a 50/50 mix of melted beeswax and pine pitch to waterproof and bond the filaments together.
3. **The Flemish Eye Loop:**
   - Divide fibers into two equal bundles (each consisting of approx. 14–18 long strands).
   - Near the end, twist one bundle away from you and wrap it over the other bundle toward you (the standard reverse-twist technique).
   - Form an 8 cm length of tight two-ply rope. Bend it back on itself into a 25 mm loop (the top eyelet).
   - Braid the tails back into the main standing bundles with reverse twists. Under tension, the friction locks the eyelet permanently without slipping.
4. **The Timber Hitch Base:** The bottom end of the string is tied to the lower bow nock with a self-cinching **Timber Hitch** (Bowyer's Knot), allowing micro-adjustments to the brace height (target: 15 cm / 6 inches between string and grip).

---

## 4. Arrow Crafting & Lethal Broadhead Hafting

An imperfect bow with perfect arrows shoots accurately; a magnificent bow with crooked arrows cannot hit a target at 10 paces.

1. **Shaft Selection:** Harvest straight, yearling shoots of **Wild Rose, Dogwood, Viburnum (Arrowwood), or River Cane (Bamboo)**. Thickness: 8 to 9 mm.
2. **Heat Straightening:** Warm crooked kinks over hot campfire coals for 15 seconds. Wood lignins soften at 80°C. Bend the shaft straight with your hands, hold for 10 seconds until cool, and the wood sets permanently straight.
3. **Fletching (Flight Stabilization):**
   - Split primary wing flight feathers from turkeys or geese down the central quill with a razor.
   - Cut three matching 10 cm vanes.
   - Bind them at 120° intervals around the rear shaft using fine thread or sinew, oriented so the "cock feather" points perpendicular to the bow riser.
4. **Flintknapping & Hafting Broadheads:**
   - Knap a 5 cm triangular arrowhead from high-silica flint, chert, or green bottle glass using an antler pressure flaker, creating sharp, serrated cutting edges.
   - Saw a 20 mm deep notch into the front tip of the wooden arrow shaft.
   - Melt pine pitch glue ($70\%\text{ pine resin} + 20\text{ pulverized charcoal} + 10\%\text{ dry beeswax/fat}$). Fill the notch with hot pitch and seat the broadhead tang.
   - Wrap the junction tightly with wet deer sinew. As sinew dries, it contracts with massive hydraulic force, locking the broadhead into an indestructible, glass-cutting hunting tip.

guides.summary: Comprehensive manual on building continuous-yield physical and biological water filters: multi-strata gravel/sand/charcoal columns, activated biochar adsorption, and microporous clay-sawdust ceramic pot purifiers.
guides.content:
While chemical disinfection (bleach, iodine) and boiling neutralize microbial pathogens, they do not remove heavy turbidity, suspended sediment, agricultural pesticides, radioactive fallout particles, or foul tastes. Conversely, coarse straining alone leaves viruses and bacteria intact.

A complete survival water system uses physical filtration first to eliminate turbidity and chemical toxins, followed by biological filtration or terminal disinfection. Below are four field-constructible filtration systems ranging from emergency field columns to permanent village-scale ceramic filters.

---

### System 1: The Multi-Layer Gravity Biosand Column

The multi-layer gravity column reproduces natural subterranean aquifer filtration. It combines mechanical particle entrapment, electrostatic attraction, and biological digestion (the *Schmutzdecke* biolayer).

#### 1. Filter Strata Layout
A tall, narrow container (5-gallon bucket, 10-liter water container, or section of 100mm PVC / clay drainage pipe) is loaded with four distinct stratified layers from bottom to top:

```
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ TOP: 5-8 cm Standing Water Head (Maintains pressure)   │
├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ LAYER 4 (Top): Fine Washed Silica Sand (25-30 cm)      │
│ → Mechanical particulate trap & Schmutzdecke bio-film │
├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ LAYER 3: Crushed Pyrolyzed Activated Charcoal (10 cm)  │
│ → Adsorbs chemicals, pesticides, tannins, odors        │
├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ LAYER 2: Coarse Sand / Grit (5 cm)                     │
│ → Prevents charcoal from migrating downward            │
├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ LAYER 1 (Bottom): Washed Pea Gravel / Small Stones     │
│ → Surrounds perforated outlet pipe; prevents clogging  │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

#### 2. Technical Blueprint

#### 3. Assembly & Sand Preparation
1. **Sand Washing (Critical):** Never use unwashed beach sand (excess salt) or builders' sand with chemical plasticizers. Gather quartz or river sand. Rinse in clean water 10+ times until wash water is crystal clear. Boil sand in iron pot to eliminate pathogens.
2. **Preparing the Charcoal:** Use pure hardwood charcoal (never chemical briquettes with petroleum binders). Crush charcoal into 1–3 mm granules using a wooden mallet. Sieve out dust. Rinse thoroughly.
3. **Layer Packing:** Drill five 3 mm drainage holes in the container base. Cover holes with clean cloth, porous canvas, or wire mesh. Add gravel layer (6 cm), coarse sand (5 cm), charcoal (10 cm), and fine silica sand (25 cm). Compact each layer gently with a flat wooden stamper to prevent channeling paths.
4. **Diffuser Plate:** Cut a round piece of plastic or tin with tiny pinholes, placed 2 cm above the top sand layer. When pouring raw water, the plate prevents the water jet from disturbing the fine sand bed.
5. **Schmutzdecke Cultivation:** Over 10–14 days of continuous operation, a living biological gelatinous layer forms on the top 1 cm of sand. This bio-film consumes pathogenic bacteria (*E. coli*, *Salmonella*, *Cholera*) biologically, reducing viral counts by up to 90%.

---

### System 2: Steam-Activated Biochar Adsorption

Standard campfire charcoal has limited surface area. "Activated" carbon undergoes chemical or steam oxidation at red heat, opening billions of microscopic sub-nanometer pores to adsorb heavy metals, chlorine, pharmaceuticals, and synthetic pollutants.

#### 1. Kiln Production Procedure
1. Pack a sealed steel can (e.g., paint can with a 2 mm vent hole) with dried dense hardwood chips (Oak, Hickory, Beech).
2. Place the can into the center of a roaring fire ($700^\circ\text{C}$ to $800^\circ\text{C}$) for 2 hours. Volatile wood gases will jet out of the hole and burn.
3. Once the flame at the vent dies, steam activate by injecting a fine spray of boiling water/steam through the vent hole into the red-hot charcoal, or immediately submerge the red-hot charcoal into a sealed pot containing a $25\%$ calcium chloride or clean brine solution.
4. Wash the cooled biochar with clean water and dry. This increases internal surface area from $2\,\text{m}^2/\text{g}$ to over $500\,\text{m}^2/\text{g}$.

---

### System 3: Porous Clay-Sawdust Ceramic Pot Filter

Developed for village-scale off-grid filtration, ceramic pot filters physically block 99.9% of all bacteria, protozoa, and parasitic ova without requiring electricity or chemical supplies.

#### 1. Material Formula
* **Terracotta Red Clay:** 50% by volume, pulverized and sifted through a fine mesh (removes pebbles).
* **Fine Combustible Sifted Sawdust (or Rice Husks):** 50% by volume. The sawdust particles must be $<1\,\text{mm}$.
* **Clean Water:** Added gradually until the clay-sawdust mixture reaches workable plastic molding consistency.

#### 2. Fabrication & Firing Protocol
1. **Forming:** Press the clay-sawdust dough into a flower-pot-shaped mold (open top, flat circular base, 20 cm diameter, 25 cm height). Maintain uniform 1.5 cm wall thickness throughout.
2. **Drying:** Air-dry slowly under shade for 7–10 days, followed by 3 days in direct sun. Fast drying causes structural shrinkage cracks.
3. **Firing (The Pyrolysis Burnout):** Place dried pots inside a closed brick kiln or adobe clamp kiln. Slowly raise temperature over 6 hours to $900^\circ\text{C}$ ($1,650^\circ\text{F}$) using hardwood charcoal and bellows.
   - At $400^\circ\text{C}$, the embedded sawdust particles combust, vaporize, and vent out, leaving behind millions of microscopic tortuous interconnected pores (1 to 3 microns in diameter).
   - At $900^\circ\text{C}$, the clay vitrifies into rigid waterproof ceramic stoneware.
4. **Colloidal Silver Impregnation (Optional Enhancement):** Paint the interior and exterior of the fired pot with a dilute solution of colloidal silver (or brush with crushed silver nitrate). Silver ions bond to the ceramic, functioning as a continuous biocide that kills trapped bacteria.
5. **Operation:** Suspend the ceramic pot inside a clean 20-liter receptacle with a spigot. Pour raw river or pond water directly into the pot. Clean water seeps through the porous walls at a rate of 1.5 to 2.5 liters per hour.

---

### System 4: Emergency Sapwood Xylem Filtration

When stranded in wilderness without containers or tools, the natural vascular tissue of fresh coniferous sapwood (pine, spruce, cedar, fir) can be used as a high-performance microporous filter.

#### 1. Biological Mechanism
Xylem conduits in gymnosperms (conifers) have pit membranes connecting adjacent tracheid cells. These membranes feature nanometer-scale pores (approx. 20 to 100 nm) designed to transport sap while preventing gas embolisms. These pores are naturally small enough to physically trap bacteria and protozoan cysts.

#### 2. Field Assembly
1. Cut a 3 cm long section of fresh green conifer branch (1.5 to 2 cm diameter).
2. Peel off the outer bark and cambium layer, leaving only the pale sapwood cylinder.
3. Insert the wood plug snugly into the neck of a plastic water bottle with the base cut off, or clamp it inside a flexible silicone/rubber hose. Seal edges with tree resin or tight lashing.
4. Fill the reservoir with water and apply pressure (gravity head or by squeezing the bottle). Water flows longitudinally through the wood tracheids, producing clean, pathogen-free water drop by drop.

---

### Filtration Efficacy Comparison

| System | Bacteria Removal | Virus Removal | Chemical / Heavy Metals | Flow Rate | Lifespan |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Multi-Layer Biosand Column** | 98–99% (with biolayer) | 80–90% | High (via biochar layer) | 0.5–2.0 L/hr | 1–3 Years (surface scraping required) |
| **Ceramic Clay Pot** | 99.9% | 50–70% (size exclusion) | Low (unless biochar added) | 1.5–2.5 L/hr | 2–5 Years (brush scrub every 3 months) |
| **Xylem Wood Plug** | 99.0% | Moderate | Low | 0.1–0.3 L/hr | 1–2 Days (dries out and cracks) |
| **Boiling Alone** | 100% | 100% | 0% (concentrates heavy metals) | Batch | Immediate |

guides.title: Solar Still Water Purifier
guides.tags: water, purification, hydration, solar, condensation, emergency
guides.summary: Construct an emergency ground-pit solar distillation apparatus to extract drinkable moisture from soil, brackish water, or non-poisonous foliage using solar thermal energy.
guides.content:
## Principle of Operation
A solar still exploits thermal evaporation and dew-point condensation. Sunlight penetrates a transparent plastic sheet, warming the soil and moisture-bearing organic matter trapped in an excavated pit. As water vapor evaporates, it separates from contaminants, heavy salts, pathogens, and particulate toxins. The rising vapor condenses against the underside of the angled plastic cone, coalescing into droplets that slide to the inverted apex and drip directly into a clean catch vessel.

```svg
<svg viewBox="0 0 700 360" width="100%" height="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">

      <stop offset="100%" stop-color="#1f2937"/>
    </linearGradient>
    <linearGradient id="sunGrad" x1="0%" y1="0%" x2="100%" y2="100%">

  <text x="350" y="343" fill="#94a3b8" font-size="11" font-family="monospace" text-anchor="middle">Yield: 0.5 - 1.5 Liters / 24 Hours in Direct Sunlight</text>

```

## Bill of Materials
- **Transparent Sheet:** 2m x 2m clear polyethylene sheeting (or clean plastic tarp/survival blanket).
- **Collection Vessel:** Wide-mouth metal canteen, cup, or clean half-canteen.
- **Drainage Straw / Siphon (Optional):** 1.5m surgical or rubber hose running outside pit to drink without breaking the air seal.
- **Center Weight:** Smooth 0.5kg stone (avoid sharp edges that pierce plastic).
- **Moisture Substrate:** Non-toxic succulent leaves, wet river sand, contaminated water, or green leafy branches.

## Step-by-Step Construction Procedure
1. **Pit Excavation:** Dig a conical hole approximately 1 meter in diameter and 60 cm deep in direct sunlight. Ensure pit walls slope inward at roughly 45 degrees.
2. **Moisture Bedding:** Line the perimeter walls and trench base with wet foliage, brackish water, or mud. **Crucial:** Keep the center pedestal clean and dry.
3. **Position Vessel:** Place your collection cup directly in the lowest center point of the pit. Ensure it stands flat and cannot tip.
4. **Air-Tight Seal:** Drape the plastic sheet across the top. Weigh down all outer edges with excavated dirt and heavy stones. The perimeter seal must be 100% airtight to trap thermal humidity.
5. **Set the Inverted Apex:** Place your smooth central stone onto the top center of the plastic directly above the mouth of the collection cup. Adjust until the cone tip hangs 5 cm above the rim.
6. **Harvest:** Allow 4–8 hours of solar exposure. Never open during peak solar hours to avoid heat loss.

guides.title: Biochar Deep-Trench Latrine
guides.tags: sanitation, cholera, dysentery, latrine, biochar, public health
guides.summary: Neutralize fecal-oral transmission vectors, flies, and dysentery pathogens by constructing a separated drainage trench charged with crushed activated charcoal and dry carbon cover.
guides.content:
## Epidemiological Principle
In non-combat disaster and collapse scenarios, **fecal-oral waterborne pathogens (Cholera, E. coli, Shigella, Typhoid) cause 80%+ of early mortalities**. Proper sanitation requires a physical barrier preventing vector access (flies) and a minimum distance of **30 meters (100 feet)** from any natural water reservoir or drinking well.

```svg

  <defs>
    <linearGradient id="soilG" x1="0%" y1="0%" x2="0%" y2="100%">
      <stop offset="0%" stop-color="#3e2723"/>
      <stop offset="100%" stop-color="#1b120c"/>
    </linearGradient>
  </defs>

  <rect x="0" y="0" width="700" height="360" fill="#090d16"/>

  <!-- Earth cross-section -->
  <path d="M0 120 L240 120 L240 290 L460 290 L460 120 L700 120 L700 360 L0 360 Z" fill="url(#soilG)"/>
  <line x1="0" y1="120" x2="700" y2="120" stroke="#795548" stroke-width="3"/>

  <!-- Latrine Trench Layers -->
  <!-- Gravel/sand drainage base -->
  <rect x="240" y="270" width="220" height="20" fill="#78909c"/>
  <text x="350" y="284" fill="#cfd8dc" font-size="10" font-family="monospace" text-anchor="middle">10cm Coarse Gravel Base</text>

  <!-- Crushed Charcoal Buffer Layer -->
  <rect x="240" y="240" width="220" height="30" fill="#212121" stroke="#424242"/>
  <text x="350" y="260" fill="#e0e0e0" font-size="11" font-family="monospace" text-anchor="middle">Crushed Biochar (Adsorption / Odor / Bacteria)</text>

  <!-- Fecal Core & Carbon Cover alternating layers -->
  <rect x="240" y="215" width="220" height="25" fill="#5d4037" opacity="0.8"/>
  <rect x="240" y="195" width="220" height="20" fill="#a1887f" stroke="#8d6e63" stroke-dasharray="3,3"/>
  <text x="350" y="210" fill="#ffecb3" font-size="10" font-family="monospace" text-anchor="middle">Wood Ash + Dry Sawdust Cover (After Each Use)</text>

  <!-- Wooden Footbridge Planks -->
  <rect x="180" y="110" width="80" height="15" fill="#8d6e63" stroke="#d7ccc8" stroke-width="1.5"/>
  <rect x="440" y="110" width="80" height="15" fill="#8d6e63" stroke="#d7ccc8" stroke-width="1.5"/>
  <text x="220" y="103" fill="#d7ccc8" font-size="10" font-family="monospace" text-anchor="middle">Foot Rest Plank</text>
  <text x="480" y="103" fill="#d7ccc8" font-size="10" font-family="monospace" text-anchor="middle">Foot Rest Plank</text>

  <!-- Fly exclusion hinged lid -->
  <line x1="230" y1="110" x2="470" y2="90" stroke="#f59e0b" stroke-width="4"/>
  <text x="350" y="80" fill="#fbbf24" font-size="11" font-family="monospace" text-anchor="middle">Fly-Tight Cover (Crucial Vector Barrier)</text>

  <!-- Water table distance requirement -->
  <line x1="50" y1="320" x2="650" y2="320" stroke="#0284c7" stroke-width="2" stroke-dasharray="6,4"/>
  <text x="350" y="340" fill="#38bdf8" font-size="12" font-family="monospace" text-anchor="middle">Min 1.5m Above Seasonal High Water Table</text>
</svg>
```

## Protocol & Maintenance
1. **Siting:** Locate at least 30 meters downwind and downhill from camp and water sources. Never dig where flooding or runoff can inundate the trench.
2. **Excavation:** Dig 40 cm wide, 1.5 to 2 meters deep, and 2 meters long for a multi-person group.
3. **Biochar Bedding:** Line the floor with 10 cm of river pebbles followed by 10 cm of crushed barbecue charcoal or camp ash. Biochar binds ammonia and eliminates odors while fostering beneficial anaerobic decomposition.
4. **The Carbon Rule:** Every single deposit must immediately be dusted with two scoops of dry wood ash, dry sawdust, or crushed charcoal. This raises pH to alkaline levels that kill pathogen cysts and completely deters blowflies.
5. **Decommissioning:** When the pit fills to within 40 cm of the surface, backfill with compacted soil and mound 15 cm above ground level to compensate for settling.

guides.title: Universal Edibility Test (UET)
guides.tags: foraging, plants, edibility, botany, toxicity, poison, starvation
guides.summary: Determine whether an unknown non-woody wild plant is non-toxic and caloric using the standardized 8-stage contact, mucosal, and ingestion protocol over a mandatory 24-hour observation cycle.
guides.content:
## Critical Rules of Australian/US Army Botanical Triage
In a post-collapse scenario, **plant poisoning causes lethal hepatic failure, respiratory paralysis, or debilitating dysentery**. Never eat unknown plants when known foods are available. **Rules of Exclusion:** Avoid plants with milky/cloudy sap, umbrella-shaped flower clusters (hemlock family), fine hair barbs, almond-like scent (cyanogenic glycosides), beans/bulbs inside pods, or three-leaf patterns.

```svg

  <defs>
    <linearGradient id="stepGrad" x1="0%" y1="0%" x2="100%" y2="100%">
      <stop offset="0%" stop-color="#1e293b"/>
      <stop offset="100%" stop-color="#0f172a"/>
    </linearGradient>
  </defs>

  <rect x="0" y="0" width="700" height="380" fill="#090d16" rx="8"/>

  <!-- Title Banner -->
  <text x="350" y="32" fill="#f59e0b" font-size="14" font-weight="bold" font-family="monospace" text-anchor="middle">THE 8-STAGE BOTANICAL TOXICITY TRIAGE</text>
  <text x="350" y="50" fill="#94a3b8" font-size="10" font-family="monospace" text-anchor="middle">Mandatory 8-Hour Fast Prior to Stage 1. Test Only ONE Plant Part at a Time.</text>

  <!-- Stage 1: Separation -->
  <rect x="30" y="70" width="140" height="75" rx="6" fill="url(#stepGrad)" stroke="#38bdf8" stroke-width="1.5"/>
  <text x="40" y="90" fill="#38bdf8" font-size="11" font-weight="bold" font-family="monospace">STAGE 1</text>

  <text x="40" y="125" fill="#94a3b8" font-size="9" font-family="monospace">Test ONLY leaves,</text>
  <text x="40" y="137" fill="#94a3b8" font-size="9" font-family="monospace">roots OR stems.</text>

  <path d="M170 107 L200 107" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#arrow)"/>

  <!-- Stage 2: Skin Contact -->
  <rect x="200" y="70" width="140" height="75" rx="6" fill="url(#stepGrad)" stroke="#38bdf8" stroke-width="1.5"/>
  <text x="210" y="90" fill="#38bdf8" font-size="11" font-weight="bold" font-family="monospace">STAGE 2 (15m)</text>
  <text x="210" y="108" fill="#f8fafc" font-size="11" font-family="sans-serif">Skin Contact</text>
  <text x="210" y="125" fill="#94a3b8" font-size="9" font-family="monospace">Rub inside elbow.</text>
  <text x="210" y="137" fill="#fca5a5" font-size="9" font-family="monospace">Watch: Rash, burn.</text>

  <path d="M340 107 L370 107" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="2"/>

  <!-- Stage 3: Lip Contact -->
  <rect x="370" y="70" width="140" height="75" rx="6" fill="url(#stepGrad)" stroke="#38bdf8" stroke-width="1.5"/>
```
